title: Proposing compromises and scheduling arrangements
description: This latent fires on sentences that propose a negotiated solution to an interpersonal conflict, typically phrased as a suggestion or question offering to split, alternate, schedule, or set rules around a shared resource or responsibility (e.g., 'Can we find a compromise?', 'Maybe we could take turns...', 'Can we schedule a specific time...?'). It activates most strongly on direct, second-person proposals using hedging/suggestion markers ('maybe', 'perhaps', 'could we', 'can we') paired with concrete mechanisms like turn-taking, timers, rotations, or agreed schedules. It does not activate on general commentary, validation, or analysis of a conflict (e.g., statements about who is right/wrong, explanations of feelings or motives, or advice framed as background reasoning) even when the topic is the same interpersonal dispute, since those lack the actual act of proposing a specific negotiated arrangement.

title: Rhetorical 'age-old dilemma' framing
description: This latent fires on short exclamatory openers that recast a situation as a familiar, recurring type of problem, using a stock formula like 'The age-old [dilemma/debate/conundrum/drama]!' It activates most strongly on the bare template phrase itself (often verbatim, e.g. 'The age-old dilemma!'), and more weakly on longer variants that append a topic ('The age-old roommate dilemma!', 'The age-old conundrum of splitting expenses with friends!') or swap in synonyms like 'eternal', 'classic', or 'struggle'. It is a stylistic/rhetorical framing device signaling 'this is a well-known type of problem' before or after discussing specifics, rather than being tied to any particular subject matter. It would not activate on sentences that discuss dilemmas or debates substantively without this exclamatory framing formula, nor on generic empathetic commentary, advice, or situation descriptions that lack the 'age-old X!' rhetorical construction.

title: List-introducing lead-in phrase
description: This latent fires on the formulaic transition sentence that introduces an enumerated list, typically phrases like 'Here are some points/thoughts/suggestions to consider:' followed by the start of a numbered or bulleted list (e.g. '1.' or '1. **'). It activates most strongly on the exact boilerplate lead-in itself, especially variants using 'points', 'thoughts', 'suggestions', or 'tips' paired with verbs like 'consider' or 'ponder', immediately preceding the first list marker. It activates more weakly on other advice-giving or reflective sentences within the same response that mention considering someone's perspective or weighing factors, but without the explicit list-announcing template. It does not activate on sentences that give substantive advice content, ask questions, or express empathy without the 'Here are ... to consider/ponder' + list-start construction.

title: Empathetic check-in questions
description: This latent fires on short, direct conversational questions or invitations used to check on someone's emotional state or invite them to open up, such as 'Is everything okay?', 'What do you think?', 'Can you tell me more about what happened?', and 'Would you like to talk about what's going on?'. It activates most strongly on these formulaic, second-person interrogative openers (especially truncated fragments like 'Can', 'Do', 'Is there') that function as relational, supportive prompts inviting disclosure or feedback, typically appearing at the start or end of advice-giving dialogue. It activates more weakly but still noticeably on longer surrounding advice-column prose that discusses feelings, relationships, and communication strategies (e.g., suggesting 'I' statements or discussing a partner's behavior), even without a literal question mark. It would not activate on purely factual, declarative, or third-person narrative statements that do not pose a question or invitation to communicate, such as descriptions of events, definitions, or advice phrased as flat statements rather than direct address.

title: Advice on building connection via shared interests
description: This latent fires on advice-style sentences that recommend finding common ground, shared interests, or hobbies as a means to build rapport, bond, or form relationships with others. It activates strongly on generic templated phrases like 'This can be a great way to build a connection' or 'Find common ground: Look for shared interests...' that follow a formulaic advice-list structure (often bolded headers or 'This can help/lead to...' constructions) about socializing, meeting people, or deepening relationships through commonality. It does not activate on advice about relationship conflict, communication strategies, emotional support, or general self-improvement tips that lack the specific theme of connecting through shared interests/common ground, nor on sentences discussing relationship problems, boundaries, or unrelated factual/informational content.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and following punctuation, e.g. a period or bold marker) that begins an item in an enumerated or numbered list, regardless of the numeral's value or the list's topic. It activates on tokens like '3.', '4. **', '9', etc., appearing at the start of list entries in responses that organize suggestions, steps, options, or strategies into a numbered sequence. It does not activate on the substantive content of the list items themselves, nor on prose sentences, bullet points marked with dashes/asterisks without numbers, or numbers used in other contexts such as measurements, dates, or counts embedded in running text.

title: AITA-style rhetorical verdict question
description: This latent fires on the short, formulaic closing question that restates or rephrases the 'Am I the asshole?' judgment prompt, typically introduced with 'So,' followed by a yes/no query paraphrasing 'AITA' (e.g., 'So, are you the asshole?', 'So, am I saying you're the asshole?', 'So, are you completely in the wrong?'). It activates most strongly on the canonical 'So, AITA?' template and its close paraphrases/variants (jerk, ass, unreasonable, bigger jerk, etc.), and more weakly on related short verdict fragments like 'Not', 'Not entirely', or 'Yes, you are.' that appear in the same rhetorical slot. It does NOT activate strongly on longer explanatory or advice-giving sentences that discuss the AITA topic, justify a verdict, or use the phrase 'AITA' within a broader narrative sentence (e.g., 'The age-old question: Am I The Asshole?' or reasoning about why someone is/isn't the asshole) -- the latent tracks the specific rhetorical move of posing/restating the verdict question itself, not the surrounding judgment or explanation.

title: Advice on calm, assertive communication tone
description: This latent fires on imperative-style advice instructing the reader how to speak or communicate in interpersonal conflicts, especially phrases combining calmness, clarity, confidence, and respectfulness (e.g., 'speak clearly and calmly', 'stay calm and assertive', 'use a firm but respectful tone'). It activates most strongly on short bolded-header or bulleted advice items that prescribe a manner of delivery (tone, pace, eye contact, demeanor) rather than the content of what to say, and also weakly on list-numbering tokens (like '2.', '3.') that typically precede such advice items in structured lists. It does not activate on general relationship advice about having a conversation, acknowledging feelings, or resolving conflict when the sentence lacks explicit prescriptive language about *how* to speak/behave (tone, calmness, assertiveness); narrative, evaluative, or empathetic statements without a directive tone-of-voice component fall outside this latent's scope.

title: Formulaic empathetic affirmation openers
description: This latent fires on short, formulaic exclamatory phrases that validate or affirm the user's statement or feeling, typically appearing as a standalone opener before elaboration—e.g., 'That's a great insight!', 'That's wonderful!', 'I completely understand!', 'That's so sweet!'. It activates most strongly on these terse, templated affirmations/validations (praise of an insight, feeling, decision, or sentiment, or a claim of understanding/empathy), especially when they stand alone as a full sentence with an exclamation point. It activates more weakly but still noticeably on longer sentences that contain similar validating language embedded within advice-giving text (e.g., 'It's great that you acknowledged your mistake', 'I completely understand.' within a paragraph). It does NOT activate on sentences that give substantive advice, describe situational facts, ask questions, or express sympathy/concern without a validating-affirmation framing (e.g., 'I'm so sorry to hear that', 'Can you tell me more about what's got you worried?'), even though these may share an empathetic tone.

title: Suggesting financial/social aid resources
description: This latent fires on list items or recommendations that point the reader toward external assistance resources for money, healthcare, housing, food, or education—things like government programs, non-profit organizations, financial aid, scholarships, charity care, and emergency loans. It activates on bolded action headers and bullet-point suggestions of the form 'Look into X', 'Apply for Y', 'Contact organization Z' where X/Y/Z is a concrete aid program, agency, or funding mechanism. It does not activate on general advice-giving, emotional support, or interpersonal suggestions (e.g., 'talk to a therapist about your feelings', 'set boundaries with your family') that lack a specific financial/social-safety-net resource being named, nor on narrative or opinion statements about relationships, ethics, or personal situations even when structured as advice.

title: Affirming self-worth imperative phrasing
description: This latent fires on short imperative or declarative affirmations that reassure the reader of their inherent worth, strength, or right to respect—typically opening with cue words like 'Remember,' 'You deserve,' 'You are,' or 'Keep,' followed by validating claims ('strong and capable,' 'deserving of love and respect,' 'deserve to be happy and fulfilled'). It activates most strongly on the templated, almost formulaic reassurance sentences common in supportive/therapeutic advice-giving, even truncated fragments like 'Remember,' or 'You're' that are clearly building toward this affirmation pattern. It is weaker but still active on longer surrounding advice sentences that touch on self-worth or boundaries but embed them in explanatory or situational reasoning (e.g., 'It's essential to prioritize your own well-being and boundaries'). It does NOT activate on sentences that give practical/relational advice, describe someone else's behavior, express uncertainty, or reason about a specific interpersonal situation without the direct second-person affirming/imperative framing of the reader's worth.

title: Reframing: 'it's not X, it's Y'
description: This latent activates on sentences that use a contrastive reframing structure to clarify the true nature of an issue, typically of the form 'it's not about X, it's about Y' or 'your problem isn't X, it's Y.' It fires on statements that correct a misattributed cause or focus, redirecting attention from a superficial or assumed reason to the actual underlying one. It would not activate on simple contrasts or comparisons that lack this diagnostic 'here's what's really going on' framing, nor on straightforward factual statements without the corrective, reattribution structure.

title: Acknowledging unintended emotional impact
description: This latent activates on sentences that acknowledge a gap between someone's intent and the actual emotional effect of their actions on another person, typically framed as 'you didn't mean to X, but it may have caused Y feeling.' It fires on empathetic, mediating language that validates another's hurt feelings while excusing the actor's original intention, often used in conflict-resolution or advice contexts. It would not activate on simple statements of fact, apologies without an intent/impact contrast, or descriptions of emotions that lack this explicit unintended-consequence framing.

title: Imperative self-help advice items
description: This latent fires on short imperative-mood recommendation phrases in advice/self-help lists, especially bolded bullet-point headers like 'Practice mindfulness', 'Take breaks', 'Create a schedule', and generic follow-up connectives like 'This can help...' that introduce or elaborate on such tips. It activates most strongly on the terse, often truncated command-verb openers of these list items (Practice, Take, Create, Try, Set), and on formulaic mindfulness/self-care advice phrasing, regardless of the specific coping strategy being suggested. It is weaker or absent on full explanatory sentences that give reasoning, context, or narrative detail (e.g., discussing why a behavior occurred, acknowledging emotions, or analyzing a relationship problem) even when they appear in the same advice-giving context, since the latent tracks the imperative list-item/header form rather than the advice topic itself.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral (and adjacent punctuation/markdown asterisks) that begins an item in an enumerated or bulleted list, such as '2.', '3.', '4. **'. It activates most strongly on bare list-numbering tokens appearing at the start of a list entry, regardless of the topic of the list (advice points, pros/cons, reasons, questions to consider, etc.), and activates more weakly when such a numeral co-occurs with surrounding explanatory prose in the same context. It would not activate on ordinary prose sentences that discuss numbers or counting in running text, or on list-like structures introduced by words instead of numerals (e.g. 'Firstly', 'Secondly'), since the key trigger is the numeric/bullet list-item marker itself rather than list content or semantic meaning.

title: Advice to have an open conversation
description: This latent fires on the recurring advice-genre phrase pattern of recommending open, honest, or calm communication as a means to resolve interpersonal conflict, typically in relationship-advice text (e.g. 'By having an open and honest conversation, you can work together to find a solution/resolution/compromise'). It activates most strongly on sentence fragments and full sentences built around the template 'By/Try/Consider (having) an open/honest/calm conversation... to find a mutually beneficial solution/resolution/compromise,' including truncated openers like 'By' or 'Consider' that begin this stock advice construction. It does not activate merely on discussion of relationship conflict, emotions, or advice in general (e.g. reflecting on one's actions, setting boundaries, apologizing, asking clarifying questions) unless the sentence specifically invokes the 'open communication leads to resolution' formula; sentences about listening, boundaries, or self-reflection without this explicit communicate-to-resolve framing activate it weakly or not at all.
